title: Korea's Tripitaka Koreana was carved into about 80,000 blocks
body: Korean carvers engraved Buddhist texts on about 80,000 woodblocks between 1237 and 1248. Special buildings at Haeinsa Temple have housed the collection since the 15th century.
takeaway: Preserving the blocks preserves the source from which another copy can be printed.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Haeinsa Temple Janggyeong Panjeon
visual: rows of stacked wooden printing blocks viewed from their uncarved edges

title: Aksum kept its coronation role after its political decline
body: Aksum was the centre of a powerful kingdom in what is now northern Ethiopia. The city declined politically in the 10th century CE, but Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned there long afterwards.
takeaway: A former capital can keep symbolic authority after the institutions that governed from it have moved on.
visual: a tall carved stone stela among the ruins of Aksum

title: Peru's Nasca figures were scratched into the ground
body: Between about 500 BCE and 500 CE, people marked large figures and geometric lines on Peru's dry coastal plain. The area containing the figures covers about 450 square kilometres.
takeaway: Seen from far above, separate stretches of cleared ground resolve into animals and other shapes.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa
visual: an overhead view of a bird-shaped geoglyph traced on the Peruvian desert

title: Poverty Point's giant earthworks were built by foragers
body: People who hunted, fished and gathered in the lower Mississippi Valley built the Poverty Point complex more than 3,000 years ago. It includes five mounds and six nested ridges around a central plaza.
takeaway: Large construction projects could bring together communities whose food came from wild resources.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point (2014)
visual: an elevated view of broad curved earthen ridges around an open grassy space
